questions.prompt: After a path is replaced by samples \(x_0,\ldots,x_N\), the decision variable of the optimization problem is
questions.explanation: Discretizing replaces the curve by finitely many numbers, and those numbers are what the problem chooses. Leaving the decision as a free function is the calculus-of-variations form, which the grid was meant to leave behind. The final time can be one coordinate of the decision, but it is not the whole decision while the samples are free. An obstacle radius is data, unless the problem is explicitly designing the obstacle.

the radius of an obstacle
the list of those samples, together with any control values the transcription keeps free

questions.prompt: Samples are \((0,\ 0)\), \((1,\ 0)\), \((1,\ 2)\), and \((4,\ 2)\). What is the smoothness cost, the sum of the squared steps between consecutive samples?
questions.explanation: The steps are \((1,\ 0)\), \((0,\ 2)\), and \((3,\ 0)\). Their squared lengths are \(1\), \(4\), and \(9\). The sum is \(14\). Reporting \(9\) keeps only the last square. Reporting \(4\) keeps only the middle square. Reporting \(3\) is the last horizontal step, not its square. The cost adds every squared step, including the vertical one.

questions.prompt: An energy cost on a control sequence \(u_0,\ldots,u_{N-1}\) is
questions.explanation: Energy here means a sum of squares of the controls, one term per interval. The obstacle count and the obstacle radius are data of the constraints, not the cost. A determinant measures volume of a linear map. It is not this cost.

the sum of the squared controls
the number of obstacles
the determinant of a dynamics matrix

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that scores one candidate path and then accepts or rejects it. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The controls are differences of the positions, so the positions come first. The squares use those controls, so they come after the controls are recovered. The subtraction uses the energy sum, so it comes after the sum. The accept-or-reject step uses that difference, so it comes last. Testing the obstacle before the positions are read, or subtracting an energy that has not been added, is not a reordering of these steps.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>two arrows from the origin</title><line x1="46" y1="102" x2="250" y2="102"/><polygon points="250,102 243.6,104.7 243.6,99.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="60.1" y1="176" x2="60.1" y2="28"/><polygon points="60.1,28 62.8,34.4 57.3,34.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="248" y="116" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="66.1" y="30" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><line x1="60.1" y1="102" x2="235.9" y2="42.3"/><polygon points="235.9,42.3 230.7,47 228.9,41.8" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="243.9" y="34.3" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">a</text><line x1="60.1" y1="102" x2="235.9" y2="161.7"/><polygon points="235.9,161.7 228.9,162.2 230.7,157" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="243.9" y="175.7" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">b</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: Two arrows leave the origin, one above the axis and one below.
steps: Read the candidate positions in time order.
From each position just read and the next one, recover the control on that interval as their difference divided by the time step.
Square the controls just recovered and add the squares to produce the energy.
Subtract that energy from the best energy stored so far.
Accept the candidate only when the difference just computed is positive and every position that entered the energy lies outside the obstacle.

questions.prompt: Which of these feasible sets are nonconvex?
questions.explanation:
A set is nonconvex when some segment between its points leaves the set.
• The outside of a disk fails: \((-2,\ 0)\) and \((2,\ 0)\) are both at distance \(2\) from the origin, and the segment between them passes through the origin.
• The union of two disjoint intervals fails: the segment from \(1\) to \(3\) leaves the union.
• A disk, a half-space, and a box are convex. Every segment between their points stays inside.

options: the outside of a disk, \(\lVert x\rVert \ge 2\)
the inside of a disk, \(\lVert x\rVert \le 2\)
the half-space \(x_1 \ge 0\)
the union of the two intervals \([0,\ 1]\) and \([3,\ 4]\) on the line

questions.prompt: Samples on a line sit at \(0\), at \(s\), and at \(4\). The smoothness cost is \(w\) times the sum of the two squared steps. That cost equals
questions.explanation: The steps are \(s - 0\) and \(4 - s\). The sum of squares is \(s^2 + (4 - s)^2\), and the weight \(w\) multiplies that sum. Both names appear. Dropping \(w\) leaves the unweighted sum. Using only \(s^2\) drops the second step. Replacing \(4 - s\) by \(4 + s\) points the second step the wrong way.

questions.prompt: A note averages two paths around a disk of radius \(1\) centered at \((1,\ 0)\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The two paths and their samplewise average are as stated. The middle sample of the average is \((1,\ 0)\), the same point as the disk's center, so the distance is \(0\), not \(2\). A disk of radius \(1\) contains that sample. Path A passes through \((1,\ 2)\), at distance \(2\) from the center, and path B through \((1,\ -2)\), also at distance \(2\). Both clear the disk, including the shared endpoints, which sit at distance \(1\). Their average does not. The outside of the disk is not convex.

questions.figure_alt: Two arrows leave the origin, one above the axis and one below.
steps: Path A uses the samples \((0,\ 0)\), \((1,\ 2)\), and \((2,\ 0)\).
The middle sample of the average is at distance \(2\) from \((1,\ 0)\), so it lies outside the disk.
reasons: The middle sample of the average is the center \((1,\ 0)\), at distance \(0\), so it lies inside the disk.
Path A does not use the sample \((1,\ 2)\).

questions.prompt: The controls on three intervals are \(2\), \(-1\), and \(2\). What is the energy, the sum of the squared controls?
questions.explanation: The squares are \(4\), \(1\), and \(4\). The sum is \(9\). The sign of the middle control disappears when it is squared. Reporting \(3\) adds the controls themselves, \(2 + (-1) + 2\). Reporting \(4\) keeps a single square. Reporting \(2\) is one control. Energy adds every square.

questions.prompt: Obstacle constraints make a trajectory problem nonconvex because
questions.explanation: Two paths can clear an obstacle on opposite sides while the segment between them hits the obstacle, so the feasible set is not convex. A sum of squares is convex, not nonconvex. A linear equality is an affine set, which is convex. The outside of one obstacle is the complement of a convex set, not a union of convex sets, and a union of convex sets need not be convex anyway.

options: the outside of an obstacle is not a convex set: the segment between two clear points can cut through the obstacle
a sum of squared controls is a nonconvex function
a linear dynamics constraint \(x_{+} = A x + B u\) is a nonconvex set
every union of convex sets is convex, and an obstacle is a union

questions.prompt: On a grid of \(N\) intervals with a free time step \(h > 0\), a minimum-time cost is
questions.explanation: With a fixed interval count, the duration is the count times the step, so minimizing time is minimizing \(h\), or \(N h\). The sum of squared controls is an energy cost. The obstacle count is data. A determinant is not a duration.

questions.prompt: The dynamics are \(x_{k+1} = 2 x_k + u_k\), with \(x_0 = 1\) and controls \(u_0 = 0\), \(u_1 = 1\). What is \(x_2\)?
questions.explanation: The first step is \(2 \cdot 1 + 0 = 2\). The second step is \(2 \cdot 2 + 1 = 5\). Reporting \(2\) stops at \(x_1\). Reporting \(1\) is the initial state, or the second control. Reporting \(3\) adds the controls to the initial state and forgets the doubling. Each step multiplies the current state by \(2\) before adding the control.

questions.prompt: This transcription, compared with a controller that applies only the first computed input and builds the problem again at the next sample,
questions.explanation: The decision is the whole sequence, chosen once. Replanning at the next sample, and applying only the first input, is a receding-horizon loop wrapped around a transcription of this kind. Dynamics are ordinary constraints of the transcription. The cost can be time or a smoothness sum. It does not have to be a sum of squares.
